entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 10 Re 10:1-11 . Vision of the Little Book. As an episode was introduced between the sixth and seventh seals, so there is one here ( Re 10:1-11:14 ) after the sixth and introductory to the seventh trumpet ( Re 11:15 , which forms the grand consummation). The Church and her fortunes are the subject of this episode: as the judgments on the unbelieving inhabiters of the earth ( Re 8:13 ) were the exclusive subject of the fifth and sixth woe-trumpets. Re 6:11 is plainly referred to in Re 10:6 below; in Re 6:11 the martyrs crying to be avenged were told they must "rest yet for a little season" or time: in Re 10:6 here they are assured, "There shall be no longer (any interval of) time"; their prayer shall have no longer to wait, but ( Re 10:7 ) at the trumpet sounding of the seventh angel shall be consummated, and the mystery of God (His mighty plan heretofore hidden, but then to be revealed) shall be finished. The little open book ( Re 10:2 , 9, 10 ) is given to John by the angel, with a charge ( Re 10:11 ) that he must prophesy again concerning (so the Greek) peoples, nations, tongues, and kings: which prophecy (as appears from Re 11:15-19 ) affects those peoples, nations, tongues, and kings only in relation to Israel and the Church, who form the main object of the prophecy. 1. another mighty angel-- as distinguished from the mighty angel who asked as to the former and more comprehensive book ( Re 5:2 ), "Who is worthy to open the book?" clothed with a cloud-- the emblem of God coming in judgment. a-- A, B, C, and Aleph read "the"; referring to ( Re 4:3 ) the rainbow already mentioned. rainbow upon his head-- the emblem of covenant mercy to God's people, amidst judgments on God's foes. Resumed from Re 4:3 (see on Re 4:3 ). face as ... the sun-- ( Re 1:16 ; 18:1). feet as pillars of fire-- ( Re 1:15 ; Eze 1:7 ). The angel, as representative of Christ, reflects His glory and bears the insignia attributed in Re 1:15 , 16 ; 4:3 , to Christ Himself. The pillar of fire by night led Israel through the wilderness, and was the symbol of God's presence.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19204"/><div sID="gen41794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19204"/><hi type="bold">2. he had--</hi>Greek, "Having."<div eID="gen41794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his hand--</hi>in his left hand: as in <reference osisRef="Rev.10.5">Re 10:5</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Rev.10.5">Re 10:5</reference>), he lifts up his right hand to heaven.<div eID="gen41795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a little book--</hi>a roll little in comparison with the "book" (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.1">Re 5:1</reference>) which contained the whole vast scheme of God's purposes, not to be fully read till the final consummation. This other, a less book, contained only a portion which John was now to make his own (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.9">Re 10:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.11">11</reference>), and then to use in prophesying to others. The New Testament begins with the word "book" (Greek, "biblus"), of which "the little book" (Greek, "biblaridion") is the diminutive, "the little bible," the Bible in miniature.<div eID="gen41796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the sea ... earth--</hi>Though the beast with seven heads is about to arise out of the sea (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>), and the beast with two horns like a lamb (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.11">Re 13:11</reference>) out of the earth, yet it is but for a time, and that time shall no longer be (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">Re 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.7">7</reference>) when once the seventh trumpet is about to sound; the angel with his right foot on the sea, and his left on the earth, claims both as God's, and as about soon to be cleared of the usurper and his followers. <div eID="gen41797" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19205"/><div sID="gen41798" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19205"/><hi type="bold">3. as ... lion--</hi>Christ, whom the angel represents, is often so symbolized (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.5">Re 5:5</reference>, "the Lion of the tribe of Juda").<div eID="gen41798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven thunders--</hi>Greek, "the seven thunders." They form part of the Apocalyptic symbolism; and so are marked by the article as well known. Thus thunderings marked the opening of the seventh seal (<reference osisRef="Rev.8.1">Re 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.5">5</reference>); so also at the seventh vial (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.17">Re 16:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.16.18">18</reference>). Wordsworth calls this the prophetic use of the article; "the thunders, of which more hereafter." Their full meaning shall be only known at the grand consummation marked by the seventh seal, the seventh trumpet (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.19">Re 11:19</reference>), and the seventh vial.<div eID="gen41799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uttered their--</hi>Greek, "spake their own voices"; that is, voices peculiarly their own, and not now revealed to men. <div eID="gen41800" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19206"/><div sID="gen41801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19206"/><hi type="bold">4. when--</hi>Aleph reads, "Whatsoever things." But most manuscripts support English Version.<div eID="gen41801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uttered their voices--</hi>A, B, C, and Aleph omit "their voices." Then translate, "had spoken."<div eID="gen41802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>omitted by A, B, C, Aleph, and Syriac.<div eID="gen41803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seal up--</hi>the opposite command to <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Re 22:20</reference>. Even though at the time of the end the things sealed in Daniel's time were to be revealed, yet not so the voices of these thunders. Though heard by John, they were not to be imparted by him to others in this book of Revelation; so terrible are they that God in mercy withholds them, since "sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." The godly are thus kept from morbid ponderings over the evil to come; and the ungodly are not driven by despair into utter recklessness of life. Alford adds another aim in concealing them, namely, "godly fear, seeing that the arrows of God's quiver are not exhausted." Besides the terrors foretold, there are others unutterable and more horrifying lying in the background. <div eID="gen41804" type="x-p"/>

Alford adds another aim in concealing them, namely, "godly fear, seeing that the arrows of God's quiver are not exhausted." Besides the terrors foretold, there are others unutterable and more horrifying lying in the background.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19208"/><div sID="gen41806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19208"/><hi type="bold">6. liveth for ever and ever--</hi>Greek, "liveth unto the ages of the ages" (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Da 12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen41806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">created heaven ... earth ... sea, &c.--</hi>This detailed designation of God as the Creator, is appropriate to the subject of the angel's oath, namely, the consummating of the mystery of God (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.7">Re 10:7</reference>), which can surely be brought to pass by the same Almighty power that created all things, and by none else.<div eID="gen41807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that there should be time no longer--</hi>Greek, "that time (that is, an interval of time) no longer shall be." Not as English Version implies, Time shall end and eternity begin. <div eID="gen41808" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19209"/><div sID="gen41809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19209"/><hi type="bold">7. But--</hi>connected with <reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">Re 10:6</reference>. "There shall be no longer time (that is, delay), but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to (so the Greek) sound his trumpet (so the Greek), then (literally, 'also'; which conjunction often introduces the consequent member of a sentence) the mystery of God is finished," literally, "has been finished"; the prophet regarding the future as certain as if it were past. A, C, Aleph, and Coptic read the past tense (Greek, "etelesthee"). B reads, as English Version, the future tense (Greek, "telesthee"). "should be finished" (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15-Rev.11.18">Re 11:15-18</reference>). Sweet consolation to the waiting saints! The seventh trumpet shall be sounded without further delay.<div eID="gen41809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mystery of God--</hi>the theme of the "little book," and so of the remainder of the Apocalypse. What a grand contrast to the "mystery of iniquity Babylon!" The mystery of God's scheme of redemption, once hidden in God's secret counsel and dimly shadowed forth in types and prophecies, but now more and more clearly revealed according as the Gospel kingdom develops itself, up to its fullest consummation at the end. Then finally His servants shall praise Him most fully, for the glorious consummation of the mystery in having taken to Himself and His saints the kingdom so long usurped by Satan and the ungodly. Thus this verse is an anticipation of <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15-Rev.11.18">Re 11:15-18</reference>.<div eID="gen41810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">declared to--</hi>Greek, "declared the glad tidings to." "The mystery of God" is the Gospel glad tidings. The office of the prophets is to receive the glad tidings from God, in order to declare them to others. The final consummation is the great theme of the Gospel announced to, and by, the prophets (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.3.8">Ga 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen41811" type="x-p"/>

His finding the roll sweet to the taste at first, is because it was the Lord's will he was doing, and because, divesting himself of carnal feeling, he regarded God's will as always agreeable, however bitter might be the message of judgment to be announced.
